messages.subject: Re: ddply() drops a number of subsets with large data
messages.subject_clean: ddply() drops a number of subsets with large data
messages.body_plain:
I'm chasing a hunch that the bug is caused by the number of possible subsets defined by the data structure. I have 10 columns, which if all of their levels were fully crossed would lead to

max(cumprod(apply(fake.data[,1:10], 2, max)))
[1] 1.880338e+16

Possible subsets. But, there are actually only 7,730 actual subsets in the data.

If I paste together the values from these 10 columns into one ID column, the bug goes away.

#########
speaker.id <http://speaker.id> <- c("Name", "Age", "Sex", "Ethnicity", "Education",  "Street", "File", "DOB", "Year")
fake.data$ID <- with(fake.data, paste(
             Name, Age,  Sex, Ethnicity, Education, Street, Year, File, DOB, VClass,
             sep = "_"))
length(unique(fake.data$ID))
## [1] 7730

means3.df <- ddply(fake.data, .(ID), summarise, value = mean(value), .progress = "text")
nrow(means3.df)
## [1] 7730

means4.df <- ddply(fake.data, c(speaker.id <http://speaker.id>, "VClass"), summarise, value = mean(value), .progress = "text")
nrow(means4.df)
## [1] 4776
#########

If I drop Sex, which has two levels, halving the number of possible subsets, the bug is mitigated.

#########
speaker.id2 <- c("Name", "Age", "Ethnicity", "Education",  "Street", "File", "DOB", "Year")
means5.df <- ddply(fake.data, c(speaker.id2, "VClass"), summarise, value = mean(value), .progress = "text")
nrow(means5.df)
## [1] 7482
#########

After Sex, the factor with the fewest unique values is Education, which has 20. Dropping education, or any one of the remaining factors eliminates the bug altogether.

-Joe

messages.body_plain:
Sure.

On a fresh install of R, open up R and from the GUI run install.packages('plyr'); it errors.

After installing xcode, download the package source from cran, navigate in the terminal to the directory where it is located, and run R CMD install plyr_1.6.tar.gz. cheers
david.

messages.body_plain:
I got 106 rows, the length of the series; how many did you get? Were
you expecting 53 x 2? If you recall, the series object in your list
had a length of 106.

I'm wondering if you were expecting that the frequency, times, etc.
would be carried along for the ride; if so, the answer is no, unless
you write a function that extracts such information from the
Time-Series object such that it can be shipped to a data frame as a
return value. (I don't know whether or not it can, but str() of your
ts object wasn't encouraging.) This is why you were encouraged in
another post on R-help to think about using the zoo, xts and/or
quantmod packages. They are better equipped to handle and manipulate
time series data in various ways. Among people who analyze time series
data in R on a regular basis, very few of them use the ts class; most
of what I've seen on R-help or in time series lecture notes are the
zoo, xts and quantmod packages or the finMetrics library. All of these
are well documented; since xts and quantmod depend on zoo, it's better
to start by learning the zoo package. It has five vignettes and a demo
to get you started. xts has a vignette and quantmod has a demo; both
are geared toward financial time series, though. A book can be
downloaded from the finMetrics web site if you prefer to go that route
(it's long, though :)

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Firstly, thank you for the reproducible example. You don't really need
Hmisc here; the rename() function in the reshape package also works.
Assuming that James' solution is what you wanted, here's a pure
plyr/reshape way to do it, as Hadley gets sad when we mix **ply with
apply family functions, and we certainly don't want that :)

library('reshape')
library('plyr')
biovo <- llply(bio, function(d) subset(d, visit == 'V0'))
biovo <- llply(biovo, rename, c(result = 'baseline', visit = 'visit0'))
bioall <- llply(bio, subset, visit != "V0")
# join() assumes left joins by default
#  => no need for an all.x = argument
out <- llply(names(bioall), function(x) join(bioall[[x]], biovo[[x]],
by = 'subjid'))
# a little post-merge cleanup:
llply(out, function(d) mutate(d, diff = result - baseline, visit0 = NULL))

After seeing all of these llply() machinations, it seems more
efficient to code all of this up into a function that can be processed
in one call:

f <- function(d)  {
#    require('reshape')
#    require('plyr')
    d1 <- subset(d, visit == 'V0')
    d2 <- subset(d, visit != 'V0')
    d1 <- rename(d1, c(result = 'baseline', visit = 'visit0'))
    dm <- join(d2, d1, by = 'subjid')
    dm <- mutate(dm, diff = result - baseline, visit0 = NULL)
    dm
   }

llply(bio, f)

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: map per row
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Your code returns a list, but you evidently want a matrix. Therefore,
your function should return a numeric vector rather than a data frame,
as follows:

> u <- daply(df, .(id), function(d) with(d, c(xy = x/y, xz = x/z)))
> u

id     xy        xz
  1 0.500 0.3333333
  3 0.800 0.6666667
  5 0.875 0.7777778

One of the keys to understanding how the **ply() functions work is to
make sure, whenever possible, that the input argument of the function
you want to pass has the same class as the input class (here d =
data.frame) and the output of the function has the same class as the
output class (a = array, which covers numeric vectors (1D), matrices
(2D) or arrays (>= 2D)).

An exception to this rule may apply when inputting or outputting
lists; in that event, the class of the input argument is that of a
generic list component if one is reading from a list, whereas the
output should conform to the output class (perhaps that of a generic
list component if a list is the output class). These little nuances in
plyr can drive you up the wall if you're not alert :)

This should be significantly faster than your version because data
frames have a lot of overhead, but if it's still not fast enough, then
look into the data.table package. For this problem, you'd do the
following:

library('data.table')
# convert a data frame to a data table
> dt <- data.table(df)
# output the (list) of two named variables xy and xz as defined
# the initial comma after the left bracket is not a typo.
> dt[, list(xy = x/y, xz = x/z)]
        xy        xz
[1,] 0.500 0.3333333
[2,] 0.800 0.6666667
[3,] 0.875 0.7777778

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The trick when calling a function in connection with a **ply()
function is that the input argument to the function should be of the
same type as the input specified by **ply (in this case, d) and the
output object from the function should be the same type as the output
type specified by **ply. [The exception to this rule applies to
*lply().] In your case, ddply => your function should have a data
frame input and a data frame output. Your function input a data frame
but output an atomic vector. You should do the transform inside the
function and then output the transformed data frame, as follows:

my.lag1 <- function(df){
    df <- df[order(df$year.x),]
    res0 <- c(NA,df$democracy)

    df$democracy.l1 <- res0[-length(res0)]
    df
}

Notice that everything is done inside the function. An alternative
version using pure plyr tools is the following:

my.lag2 <- function(df){
    df <- arrange(df, year.x)
    res0 <- c(NA,df$democracy)
    mutate(df, democracy.l1 = res0[-length(res0)])
}

arrange() is the plyr equivalent of df[order(df$blah), ]; mutate() is
the plyr equivalent of transform, with the added feature that you can
define a new variable in mutate() and then use it in subsequent
variable definitions within the same call (a very handy feature, BTW).
Then,

u <- ddply(merged5, .(country.x), my.lag1)
v <- ddply(merged5, .(country.x), my.lag2)
identical(u, v)
# [1] TRUE
head(u)    # to check that it worked.

The general form of a ddply() call is

ddply(dataFrame, .(grouping variables), function, extra arguments to function)

This is analogous to the apply family of functions, which allows one
to add optional arguments after the function is declared; e.g.,
apply(mat, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE). It's easy to forget this point (I
certainly have), so I've found it convenient to do as much as possible
inside the function body and return (in this case) a data frame to
ddply(). Hopefully this point clarifies why your ddply() function call
didn't work and gives you a little more insight into its syntax.

Side note: Thank you for using dput(), but...some subscribers read
e-mail through their cell phones and a submission of the length you
provided might not enamor you to such users because of bandwidth
limitations. I would kindly suggest that if you want to make available
a data set of this length, put it up on a web site instead (in dput()
form if you wish, but other formats are fine [and probably preferred
since R has several functions to read files directly from the web])
and include the link in your mail or, alternatively,  attach the
data/dput to the e-mail as a separate text file.

Just in case...to read dput() output from an external file, use
dget('dputfile').

HTH,
Dennis

If you want printed tables of regression summaries, then look into any
of the following:
    (i) the xtable package, which produces tables from output of
certain types of model objects (e.g., lm) and exports to LaTeX
(generally through Sweave) or html;
    (ii) the latex() function in the Hmisc package, which generates
LaTeX code to be inserted later into a LaTeX program;
    (iii) the memisc package.
There may be others.

xtable contains functions that are designed to render a pretty-printed
table inside a LaTeX document or an HTML document. The latex()
function in Hmisc generates LaTeX code for a given type of table. For
table printing to the R console, the remix package is a reasonable
option, but I wouldn't recommend it for use inside a document; try
example(remix) after the package is installed and loaded to see what
it outputs.

I haven't used memisc yet, but a quick survey indicates that it might
be the most appropriate for your needs, as it appears the package
author is in political science and most of the data sets and examples
in the package are in that area. Several users on R-help have also
recommended it in the past, so it does seem to have a fan base. plyr
is meant for summarizing/organizing/processing data by groups, not
pretty printing, although it's possible to write a function that sets
up the pretty printing inside the function body for export elsewhere
(such as an external file), in which case the plyr function to use
would likely be l_ply().

My suggestion: read the memisc documentation (it comes with a vignette
and demo). Find out at which stage the table is generated by the
appropriate memisc function - i.e., during the model fit or afterward.
Write a function whose input argument is a data frame; fit a model and
call the memisc function that returns the (code to produce the) table.
If you intend to export the (code for the) tables to a list object,
then return the table (code); if you need to export the table (code)
to an external file, then the last line of the function has to be some
type of write function with a file name - there are several ways the
file name could be specified. This might be the trickiest part. Then
use dlply() to output to a list object or d_ply() to export the tables
elsewhere.

Dennis

Hi Antonio,

Here's how I'd attack your problem:

option(digits = 2)
models <- list(
  model.b = model.b, model.b1 = model.b1,
  model.c = model.c,
  model.d = model.d,
  model.e = model.e,
  model.f = model.f,
  model.g = model.g,
  model.h = model.h, model.h1 = model.h1)

model_sum <- function(x) {
  t_table <- summary(x)$tTable
  data.frame(parameter = rownames(t_table), unrowname(t_table[, 1:2]))
}

model_sums <- ldply(models, model_sum)
names(model_sums) <- c("model", "parameter", "estimate", "se")
# That form of the data will be easiest to plot.
# e.g.

library(ggplot2)
qplot(parameter, estimate, data = model_sums, colour = model)
qplot(estimate, model, data = model_sums) + facet_wrap(~parameter,
scales = "free_x")

# But if you want a table where it's easier to compare the numbers,
# use reshape2

library(reshape2)
modelm <- melt(model_sums, id = c("model", "parameter"))
dcast(modelm, variable + parameter ~ model)

Hadley
